intro: How North American meters are read. Three standards work together. C12.19 keeps everything a meter knows in numbered tables, like the pages of a binder: standard table 23 (ST 23) holds the current readings, such as the energy totals. C12.18 reads and writes those tables through the optical port, the infrared window on the meter's front, after a logon and a password. C12.22 carries the same table requests over a network.
plain: A meter in North America keeps all its information in numbered tables, like the pages of a binder: one page says who made it, another holds the energy totals. A technician can hold a reader to the front of the meter and ask for a page by its number, after giving a name and a password. The electricity company can ask for the same pages from far away, over a network.

identify.title: Say hello
identify.text: The laptop sends an Identification request at 9600 baud, 8N1 (8 data bits, no parity bit, 1 stop bit). The meter confirms each packet with one byte, 0x06 (ACK, for acknowledge), then answers. Each packet ends with a 2-byte CRC, a check value that reveals damaged bytes. This lesson leaves it out.

logon.title: Log on
logon.text: The Logon request names the user, for the meter's event log. The Security request then sends the 20-byte password. Only now may the laptop read or write protected tables.

read.title: Read the energy table
read.text: A full read of table 23, Current Register Data: the meter's energy totals. The answer is 12 bytes and a checksum. What the bytes mean is written in other tables. ST 0 says how numbers are coded, ST 21 how many there are, and ST 12 and ST 22 what they measure.

end.title: Log off
end.text: Logoff ends the session. Terminate ends the conversation on the optical port. Without them, the meter keeps the session open until a timeout.

network.title: Over the network
network.text: Later, the head-end, the utility's central computer, reads the same table with C12.22. The same request, 30 00 17, now travels inside an ACSE message: a standard envelope that names the sender and the receiver. It uses port 1153. No logon is needed: each message carries its own security.

frames.c1222-read: Send me all of table 23 (over the network)

notes.ident-ok: The answer starts with 0x00 (OK), then the protocol (0x00: C12.18), its version and its revision. Newer meters also list optional features. Next the laptop could send Negotiate (0x60 to 0x6B) for a higher speed or bigger packets. Here it keeps the defaults.
notes.c1222-read: An ACSE message (tag 0x60) on UDP or TCP port 1153. Its header names the meter (the called AP title, a network name), the head-end (the calling AP title) and this request (the calling AP invocation ID). Its user information holds EPSEM: a control byte that sets the security mode, then the same service as on the optical port, 30 00 17. In the secure modes, AES-128 in EAX' mode protects the message with a key the meter knows. It either proves who sent it and that nobody changed it, or does that and also encrypts it.
notes.c1222-table: An ACSE message back to the head-end. Its header lets the head-end match it to the request. Inside is the same answer as on the optical port: 0x00 (OK), the count, the 12 bytes of table 23 and their checksum.

stp.name: STP
stp.note: 0xEE, the start of packet, begins every packet. A 2-byte CRC (CCITT polynomial) ends it; it is not shown here.

ctrl-1.name: Control
ctrl-1.note: 0x20: the toggle bit is 1. Each side flips it with every new packet, so a packet sent twice can be spotted.

seq.name: Sequence number
seq.note: 0: no more packets follow. A message too big for one packet comes in several, counted down to 0.

len-1.name: Length
len-1.note: 0x0001: one byte of data. Numbers in the packet are sent most significant byte first.

ident.name: Identification
ident.note: 0x20: the first service of every session.

logon.name: Logon
logon.note: 0x50: start a session as a named user.

user-id.name: User ID
user-id.note: 0x0002: a number the meter writes into its event log.

password.name: Password
password.note: 20 bytes: "tech2026" and 12 spaces. It crosses the optical port in clear text.

ok.name: OK
ok.note: Response code 0x00: OK. 0x01 is a general error; 0x03 means the password in use does not allow this.

table-23.name: Table 23
table-23.note: 0x0017 = 23: ST 23, Current Register Data. Manufacturer tables add 2048: MT 23 is 0x0817.

sum-0.name: Summation 0
sum-0.note: A running total, 6 bytes, low byte first, as ST 0 of this meter says. 0x00BC614E = 12 345 678 Wh delivered: energy from the grid to the house.

sum-1.name: Summation 1
sum-1.note: 0x01E240 = 123 456 Wh received: energy the house sent to the grid.

cksum.name: Checksum
cksum.note: 0x72: the table bytes and this byte add up to 0, modulo 256.

t-st.name: ST · standard table
t-st.note: Defined by ANSI C12.19, the same in every meter. An MT, a manufacturer table, is the maker's own.

t-23.name: 23 · current register data
t-23.note: Table 23 holds the energy and demand registers the meter keeps now. This lesson reads it whole.

facts.standard: ANSI C12.18 (optical port), C12.19 (tables), C12.22 (networks); also IEEE 1701, 1377, 1703
facts.transport: Optical port at 9600 baud, 8N1; C12.22 over UDP or TCP 1153
facts.security: C12.18: a 20-byte password in clear. C12.22: AES-128 (EAX') for each message
facts.model: Tables: standard (ST 0, ST 1, ST 23 …) and manufacturer (MT, from 2048)

tips: Read ST 0 first. It says how numbers are coded and in which byte order; without it, table 23 is just bytes.
Many meters count wrong passwords and lock the port for a while. Check the password before you try again.
A table larger than one packet comes in several. Wait for sequence number 0, or read the table in parts with a partial read (0x3F: an offset and a count).
Manufacturer tables (MT, from 2048) are laid out as each maker chooses. You need the maker's documentation to read them.

playground.file: The tables this meter has. A C12.19 reader learns them from ST 0, then reads what it needs by number.
playground.st0: Read it first: how numbers are coded, in which byte order, and which tables exist.
playground.st1: Who made the meter: a 4-letter maker code, the model, hardware and firmware versions, and a serial number.
playground.procedures: Procedures, such as a demand reset or setting the clock, start with a write to ST 7. Their results come back in ST 8.
playground.st12: What each source measures: here, energy delivered and received, in Wh.
playground.st21: How many values the register tables hold. It fixes the size of ST 23.
playground.st22: Which source each summation (running total) in ST 23 comes from.
playground.st23: The table this lesson reads: two totals of 6 bytes each.
playground.mt: Manufacturer tables: their number plus 2048. The maker decides what is in them.
